articles.title: Are More AI Features Always Better? The “Smart” Ideas I Removed
articles.excerpt: When AI features became easy to add, my product backlog grew very quickly. Automatically translate every incoming message. Generate replies before the user asks. Detect customer intent. Choose a saved…
articles.body: When AI features became easy to add, my product backlog grew very quickly. Automatically translate every incoming message. Generate replies before the user asks. Detect customer intent. Choose a saved script. Send a follow-up when a conversation becomes quiet. Summarize every chat. Score every lead. Each idea sounded reasonable in isolation. Together, they would have turned a small WhatsApp Web utility into a system constantly reading, predicting, and interrupting. I removed or narrowed several of those ideas. The experience changed how I evaluate “smart” product features. Automatic translation sounded better than on-demand translation The first idea was simple: whenever a new message appears, translate it immediately. That removes a click, which is normally a good thing.

articles.title: Checking a Cost Model Against a Stranger's Config File
articles.excerpt: I wrote a cost model for streaming a mixture-of-experts model off an SSD, and the part I was proudest of was that it gated itself twice against artifacts I had nothing to do with. Gate 1 reproduced a…
articles.body: I wrote a cost model for streaming a mixture-of-experts model off an SSD , and the part I was proudest of was that it gated itself twice against artifacts I had nothing to do with. Gate 1 reproduced a third-party runtime's on-disk container byte-for-byte. Gate 2 predicted the size of a model conversion published by different people using a different tool, and came within 1.1% against a 2% tolerance. The experiment behind that post has a limitations section I now want to revisit. It listed an ambiguity in the model's config.json , bounded the damage, and moved on: dense_mlp_idx=2 is ambiguous: one dense layer, or layers 0 and 1. This takes one, which moves bytes/token by 2.4%. Immaterial to the conclusion, unresolved regardless. The bound was right. The assumption was wrong.

articles.title: Why asking for help feels harder than solving the problem yourself
articles.excerpt: I will genuinely spend an hour stuck on something before I message someone who could answer it in two minutes. Not because I'm too proud to ask. Because asking comes loaded with a whole set of quiet f…
articles.body: I will genuinely spend an hour stuck on something before I message someone who could answer it in two minutes. Not because I'm too proud to ask. Because asking comes loaded with a whole set of quiet fears that are hard to name out loud. Maybe this is something I should already know. Maybe the person is in the middle of something. Maybe the question is too small, too obvious, too much. So I keep trying. Keep googling. Keep going in circles, all to avoid the 30-second discomfort of sending a message. If you've done this, you already know it's not rational. You're trading an hour of your time to avoid a moment of vulnerability. The math doesn't work. But the feeling keeps winning. Here's what the research actually says about why.

articles.title: Your Code Knows What Changed. But Does It Know Why?
articles.excerpt: AI can write a pull request in seconds. But when that pull request touches a piece of code written three years ago, there is a much harder question: Why does this code exist? That answer might be buri…
articles.body: AI can write a pull request in seconds. But when that pull request touches a piece of code written three years ago, there is a much harder question: Why does this code exist? That answer might be buried across 47 commits, 12 pull requests, an old incident, a Slack conversation nobody remembers, and one engineer who left the company six months ago. This is becoming one of the biggest problems in AI-assisted software engineering. Because writing code is getting cheaper. Understanding code is not. The Codebase Is Not the Whole System Consider this: if ( user . isLegacy && ! featureEnabled ) { return fallback (); } Looks suspicious. Maybe it's dead code. Maybe someone forgot to clean it up.

articles.body: CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — A new era of astronomy is about to begin after NASA's newest flagship observatory leaped from the terrestrial bounds of Earth into the vastness of space this morning. NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched today (Aug. 30) on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from the Kennedy Space Center here in Florida. Liftoff occurred at 7:26 a.m. EDT (1126 GMT) at Launch Complex-39A (LC-39A). Roman is NASA's newest orbital observatory designed to add to the wealth of research and discoveries we've received from the Hubble Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope . articles.excerpt: Some imagination and an AI tool is all you need.
articles.body: As someone who grew up in the 90s, I can tell you that ringtones were once a major status symbol. It meant you had a cutting-edge phone capable of such witchcraft, after all. Unfortunately, it took less than a decade for custom ringtones to go from impressive to something most people considered tacky. The rise of smartphones and the bombardment of notifications didn’t help custom ringtones any, either. Even if not as popular as they once were, ringtones are still a great way to add a little flair to your phone, as long as you don’t go overboard. These days, there are tons of sources for ringtones, from dedicated apps to websites that allow you to download ringtone files. Many phones can even take full tunes you own and automatically cut them into ringtones.

articles.title: This Week In Space podcast: Episode 225 — Get a Grip!
articles.excerpt: On Episode 225 of This Week In Space, Rod Pyle and Tariq Malik are joined by Adam Kall of KMI to discuss their work on the ISS may provide answers for orbital debris mitigation.
articles.body: On Episode 225 of This Week In Space , Rod Pyle and Tariq Malik are joined by Adam Kall of KMI to discuss their work on the ISS, the goals of the company, and how nature — via the humble octopus and gecko lizards — may provide answers for orbital debris mitigation. The mitigation of orbital debris is an increasingly serious problem that has not gotten enough attention, but this is changing. Commercial companies are addressing orbital debris, and one of them, KMI Space, has flown its experiments aboard the International Space Station, performing over 170 individual rendezvous-and-grab operations. The results are very promising, and the company is moving ahead with ever more ambitious designs. Download or subscribe to this show at: https://twit.tv/shows/this-week-in-space .

articles.title: When is the next lunar eclipse?
articles.excerpt: When will Earth's shadow cover the moon next following the August 2026 partial lunar eclipse?
articles.body: August's "almost Blood Moon" partial lunar eclipse has come and gone, delighting stargazers with a gorgeous natural light show as light filtered by our planet's atmosphere turned it a deep crimson around the point of maximum eclipse. But when is the next lunar eclipse ? Earth won't darken the moon again until Feb. 20, 2027, when a penumbral eclipse will cast our planet's soft outer shadow across February's full "Snow Moon" , so named for the freezing weather that occurs around the time it rises. articles.title: On this day in space! Aug. 29, 1965: NASA's Gemini 5 breaks spaceflight duration record after 2 astronauts spent '8 days in a garbage can'
articles.excerpt: On Aug. 29, 1965, two NASA astronauts returned to Earth after spending eight days in space on the record-setting Gemini 5 mission, setting the stage for longer trips to the moon.
articles.body: On Aug. 29, 1965, two NASA astronauts returned from their record-breaking Gemini 5 mission . Astronauts Gordon Cooper and Pete Conrad spent eight days in Earth orbit, and for the first time, the United States set a world record for the duration of a crewed spaceflight. The Gemini 5 mission launched on Aug. 21, 1965 atop a Titan II rocket from what was then the Cape Canaveral Air Force Station (now the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station ) in Florida. While in orbit, the astronauts were supposed to test rendezvous capabilities and maneuvers using a pod that deployed from their spacecraft. But due to an electrical problem, they had to cancel those plans along with several science experiments.

articles.title: ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude quietly get worse over time. This hidden setting fixes them
articles.excerpt: Your favorite AI chatbot might be remembering a little too much.
articles.body: I’ve been using LLM-based AI in some capacity for roughly half a decade, and in that time, the industry has changed significantly. Not only have newer competitors like Gemini and Claude arrived on the scene, but older tools like ChatGPT have also evolved dramatically. We’ve seen better third-party app integration, increased reasoning capabilities, and countless other advancements. However, I would argue that the ability to retain memories matters most. Retaining context from previous conversations helps the AI better anticipate your needs within a single session. It also allows the tool to learn more about you, ensuring that future conversations are tailored to your preferences. However, there is a real downside to memory accumulation that not everyone considers.
